sources.title: Phil Knight (Q557305) -- verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-10-23): English label 'Phil Knight', description 'American billionaire and co-founder of Nike', born 24 February 1938, no date of death, citizenship United States, Korean label '필 나이트', P18 image 'Philknightfootball.jpg'. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Phil Knight' (britannica.com), read in full via a local copy: cofounded Blue Ribbon Sports in 1964 with his former University of Oregon coach Bill Bowerman to sell Onitsuka Tiger shoes; the Stanford small-business class paper arguing that Japanese shoe production could outpace German makers; a 1962 trip to Japan to tour the Onitsuka factory; selling shoes from his car at regional track meets while working as an accountant and teaching, leaving those jobs in 1969; the split with Onitsuka in 1971 and the renaming to Nike, the swoosh logo bought for $35, the waffle-sole shoe, the 1980 public offering, the 1984 Michael Jordan contract he was 'initially reluctant' to sign, the 1988 'Just Do It' slogan, his tenure as CEO until 2004 and chair until 2016, and the late-1990s accusations of sweatshop and child-labour conditions that Britannica says were ultimately confirmed 'despite the company's initial denial', followed by announced changes, factory audits and higher minimum wages. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE. Its passages on family, political giving, philanthropy, the Laika studio and net worth were not used.

Karen Milburn, review of 'Swoosh: The Unauthorized Story of Nike and the Men Who Played There' (Julie Strasser and Laurie Becklund), The Seattle Times, 6 February 1992, read in full: reports the book's account of Knight as a recent business-school graduate going to Japan in 1962 and presenting himself as an American importer ('a serious exaggeration') to meet Onitsuka; of Blue Ribbon Sports in the 1970s writing checks against insufficient funds and relying on 'the float' until its bank relationship ended and Japanese trading company Nissho Iwai rescued it; of Knight pushing financial risk onto suppliers, sales representatives and endorsing athletes; of management dismissing the aerobics boom, after which Reebok became the No 1 athletic-shoe company in 1982, a lesson called 'expensive, and nearly fatal'; and that Knight kept control and over 40 percent of a $3 billion public company. The reviewer notes that Strasser was Nike's first advertising manager and her husband a founding manager, that Knight opposed and threatened to sue over the book (Strasser's account), and that Strasser says two or three sources corroborated most scenes. Unauthorised insider-authored account as relayed by an independent reviewer; mixed favourable/critical; the review's passages on liquor, drugs and 'outrageous behaviour' were not used.

The Oregon Encyclopedia, 'John Jaqua (1920-2009)' (oregonencyclopedia.org), the passage on Nike's founding read: in January 1964 Knight, a former University of Oregon runner, and coach Bill Bowerman met in Jaqua's living room and formed the partnership Blue Ribbon Sports, which became Nike; Jaqua helped them raise $50,000 to start; the business first imported running shoes from Japan and later manufactured shoes based on Bowerman's designs; Jaqua gave early legal help and sat on Nike's board from the start until 2004. State-history encyclopaedia, independent of Knight; the entry is about another person and is used only for the founding episode.

Brendan Dunne, feature on who brought Michael Jordan to Nike in 1984 (Complex, sneakers section; headline not recorded), 30 September 2015, read in full: competing accounts from Michael Jordan (credits George Raveling), Raveling (credits Nike's bringing Jordan to Beaverton), Sonny Vaccaro (calls himself 'the savior of Nike' and accuses Knight and Jordan of lying), Peter Moore (names Rob Strasser and Vaccaro) and Phil Knight, who downplays Vaccaro and names Moore and Strasser as the 'MVPs' and credits Tinker Hatfield for design. The article does not describe how Knight himself reached the decision. Sneaker-press feature recording disputed credit among participants; Knight's statements in it are self-reported.

William McCall (Associated Press), 'Nike chief falls short on pledge to labor, conditions worldwide unchanged, group says', The Seattle Times, 17 May 2001, read in full: the 105-page Global Exchange report assessing six promises Knight made in a May 1998 speech at the National Press Club (US indoor air-quality standards in shoe factories, minimum hiring ages of 18 and 16, NGOs in factory monitoring with published inspection results, expanded worker education, microenterprise loans for 4,000 families in four Asian countries, university research forums); the report's conclusion that the projects had 'been of little benefit to Nike workers' while crediting improved health and safety conditions; and Knight's reply that Nike had done more than any other shoe or apparel company for fair treatment of workers, that its expansion had helped raise wages, and 'I think we've made significant strides, and I'm proud of what the company's done over the last three years', with Knight and two managers noting contracts covering factories employing at least 500,000 workers in more than 50 countries. Wire report; critical report by an advocacy group with Knight's reply.

Josh Richman, 'Is Nike Still Doing It?', Mother Jones, 16 May 2001, read in full: the 115-page Global Exchange report on the six pledges from Knight's 12 May 1998 National Press Club speech, alleging that wages remained unlivable, forced overtime and intimidation persisted, monitors' visits were announced in advance and only one independent inspection (by Verite in Mexico) appeared to have occurred, and that Nike refused a living-wage standard for its roughly 530,000 workers; Nike's response from vice president Dusty Kidd that it had met most commitments (88 percent cut in petroleum-based chemicals since 1995, Verite's Mexico report made public, Fair Labor Association monitoring delayed, loans extended to 5,000 families in four countries); and Global Exchange's Jason Mark saying the company's culture had not changed. Advocacy-leaning magazine report with a company reply; counted with the Seattle Times 2001 wire as ONE perspective on the same report, and the allegations are the report's, not findings of fact by this profile.

Bill Snyder, 'Phil Knight on the Controversial Kaepernick Ad and Nike's Never-Give-Up Attitude', Stanford Graduate School of Business Insights, 14 February 2019, read in full: report on a 'View From The Top' session in which Knight traces his competitive never-give-up attitude to coach Bill Bowerman. Self-account relayed by his alma mater's school; used only to confirm the Bowerman relationship, never as support for a row, and its Kaepernick-advertising discussion was not used (cultural-political topic).

Wikimedia Commons file page 'Philknightfootball.jpg' (wikitext and API record) -- checked for the portrait's licence: photograph by Neon Tommy (USC student news site), taken 30 October 2010 at the Oregon-USC football game, imported from Flickr and passed an automated Flickr licence review on 21 March 2012 as CC BY-SA 2.0; original 2435 x 3486 pixels. Not used for any scoring.

opportunity_sensing.rationale: [src_knight_britannica, src_knight_swoosh92, src_knight_oregon | 1962-1964 | encyclopaedia + review of an unauthorised insider book + state encyclopaedia] Britannica says that in a Stanford small-business class Knight argued that Japanese shoe production, being cheaper, could outpace Germany's then-leading sneaker makers, and after graduating in 1962 he toured the Onitsuka factory and arranged to sell its Tiger shoe in the United States; the Seattle Times review of Swoosh reports that he obtained the Onitsuka meeting by presenting himself as an American importer; the Oregon Encyclopedia confirms that Blue Ribbon Sports began in January 1964 importing running shoes from Japan. A specific gap in the market was identified and acted on within two years, described by three sources of different kinds; the Stanford-paper account originates with Knight, so documented at a moderate confidence.

resourcefulness.rationale: [src_knight_britannica, src_knight_oregon, src_knight_swoosh92 | 1964-1970s | encyclopaedia + state encyclopaedia + review of an unauthorised book] Britannica says he sold the first shoes from the back of his car at regional track meets while working as an accountant and teaching at Portland State University, leaving those jobs in 1969; the Oregon Encyclopedia says Jaqua helped Knight and Bowerman raise $50,000 to start; the Seattle Times review reports that in the 1970s the company wrote checks against insufficient funds, relying on 'the float', until its bank relationship ended and Nissho Iwai rescued it, and that Knight shifted financial risk onto suppliers, sales representatives and athletes. Several independent sources show the company kept going on thin capital through improvised means; the practices are also criticised, so documented at a moderate confidence.

risk_tolerance.rationale: [src_knight_swoosh92, src_knight_britannica | 1964-1984 | review of an unauthorised insider book + encyclopaedia] The Seattle Times review of Swoosh describes the company running on overdrawn checks and 'the float' until the bank ended the relationship, and Knight pushing financial risk onto suppliers, sales representatives and endorsing athletes, while still ending up with over 40 percent of a $3 billion company; Britannica reports he left his other jobs in 1969 to concentrate on the company and signed Michael Jordan in 1984 despite initial reluctance, a deal that transformed the firm. High financial exposure repeatedly accepted and paying off is described, but the sharpest detail rests on one reviewed book by insiders who opposed and were opposed by Knight, so documented at a moderate confidence and dual-edged. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): first-pass 76 / 0.56 lowered to 70 / 0.50 because the most specific evidence comes from a single insider-authored book relayed by one review.

persistence.rationale: [src_knight_britannica, src_knight_swoosh92, src_knight_oregon | 1964-1982 | encyclopaedia + review of an unauthorised book + state encyclopaedia] Britannica describes years of part-time selling alongside two jobs, the break with Onitsuka in 1971 and the switch to the company's own Nike brand, and a later period in which the company struggled before the Jordan deal; the Seattle Times review reports that after Reebok overtook Nike in 1982 the company restructured and later regained leadership, and the Oregon Encyclopedia confirms the 1964 start. Staying with the venture through the cash crises, supplier break and market loss is documented, but the sources describe the company more than Knight's own conduct, so strong inference at a modest confidence.

collaboration.rationale: [src_knight_britannica, src_knight_oregon, src_knight_complex | 1964-1984 | encyclopaedia + state encyclopaedia + sneaker-press feature] Knight formed Blue Ribbon Sports as a partnership with Bowerman, whose shoe designs became the product (Britannica, Oregon Encyclopedia), and in the Complex feature he names Rob Strasser and Peter Moore as the 'MVPs' of the Jordan signing and credits Tinker Hatfield for design, while Sonny Vaccaro disputes this and accuses Knight of lying. A founding design-and-business partnership is well attested; the credit-sharing evidence is Knight's own statement and is contested by another participant, so strong inference at a low-to-moderate confidence.

belief_updating.rationale: [src_knight_britannica, src_knight_st01, src_knight_mj01 | 1998-2001 | encyclopaedia + wire report + magazine report] Britannica says allegations of abusive conditions and forced overtime in Nike's contract factories were ultimately confirmed despite the company's initial denial, and that in the late 1990s Knight announced changes and Nike began auditing factories and raised minimum wages; the 2001 Global Exchange report, relayed by the Seattle Times and Mother Jones, said the six pledges from his May 1998 speech fell short on several points (while crediting better health and safety conditions), and Knight replied that Nike had done more than any other shoe or apparel company and had 'made significant strides'. A documented shift from denial to announced reforms is set against a contested follow-through and a firm rebuttal, so strong inference at a low confidence, dual-edged; the report's allegations are not treated as established fact. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): kept deliberately low and dual-edged because the follow-through is disputed by the advocacy report and rebutted by Knight, and no neutral audit was read.

provenance.notes: PREFLIGHT: QID VERIFIED LIVE: Wikidata wbgetentities (2026-10-23) for Q557305 returned en label 'Phil Knight', description 'American billionaire and co-founder of Nike', born 1938-02-24, no death date, citizenship United States (Q30), kowiki label '필 나이트', P18 'Philknightfootball.jpg'; the lead's hint was correct. SLUG/QID CHECK: no candidate or production file for slug phil-knight or QID Q557305 in the roster53 worktree. REGION: north_america, nationalityCodes US. VOCABULARY: occupations entrepreneur and executive, field business, impact domains entrepreneurial, industrial and cultural, tags founder and leader and archetype entrepreneurial_builder are existing ids (cf. Akio Morita). ZERO POLITICS: Knight's political giving appears in Britannica and was not used; the Kaepernick advertising discussion in the Stanford piece was not used. LIVING SUBJECT: only documented professional business conduct is scored. EXCLUDED deliberately: family and bereavement, health, wealth, philanthropy, the Laika studio, political donations, the liquor/drugs/'outrageous behaviour' passage in the Swoosh review, the film 'Air', the Vaccaro dismissal (seen only in a search snippet), and Wikipedia/Wikidata (orientation only). The memoir 'Shoe Dog' was NOT opened; no row rests on Knight's own account alone (the Stanford GSB piece is self-account and supports no row). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Encyclopaedia Britannica 'Phil Knight' (https://www.britannica.com/biography/Phil-Knight; read in full from a local curl copy because the fetch tool returned 403). READ (8 cited non-Wikidata sources): Britannica, Seattle Times 1992 Swoosh review, Oregon Encyclopedia Jaqua entry (founding passage), Complex 2015 feature, Seattle Times/AP 2001 report, Mother Jones 2001 report, Stanford GSB 2019 piece, Commons page. Not obtained: the Oregon Encyclopedia Knight entry (URL 404), CNN's 1998 speech report (503), the primary text of Knight's 1998 speech and the Global Exchange report itself (reported only through the two 2001 press pieces), Swoosh itself, Shoe Dog. PERSPECTIVES: encyclopaedic record (Britannica); unauthorised insider-authored account relayed by an independent reviewer (opposed by Knight, with disclosed ties); state-history encyclopaedia (founding); sneaker-press feature with competing participants (Jordan, Raveling, Vaccaro, Moore, Knight); labour-advocacy report relayed by wire and magazine plus Nike and Knight replies (counted as ONE perspective); Knight's own remarks (self; never sole support). COUNTER-VOICES: the Global Exchange report, Vaccaro's dispute, and the Swoosh authors, all treated as allegations or accounts, not as established fact. LABOUR CONTROVERSY HANDLING: stated only as documented in Britannica and as the report's claims with Knight's rebuttal; no motive or character is inferred. CALIBRATION: behavioural detail is strongest for 1962-1971 but a good part rests on one reviewed book; so the highest score is 72 and the highest confidence 0.55; six rows, none padded. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): reviewed risk_tolerance (lowered 76/0.56 to 70/0.50: single insider-book dependence), belief_updating (set low and dual-edged: disputed follow-through) and collaboration (unchanged: low already, credit statements self-reported and contested); opportunity_sensing left unchanged (three independent source types). PORTRAIT: Commons 'Philknightfootball.jpg', creator Neon Tommy, CC BY-SA 2.0 with Flickr review pass, no conflicting institutional notice; downscaled only.
